utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So all the excused are present today. Prosecution, Mr. McCloskey. For the Defence teams I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Krgovic. I think that's about it. Yes. Okay. Good morning to you, Mr. Haynes and good morning to you, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later on after the first break we'll hand down an oral decision on the joint motion regarding the sequence of cross-examination and also on the Popovic motion for certification, but in the mean time let's start. Mr. Haynes, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps the easiest way to retrace our steps just a little bit is if we go back to P 377, the duty officers' notebook at page 155 in the e-court version, and page 773 in the hard copy for you, General Pandurevic. And this is an entry that relates to the morning of the 17th of July of 1995, and this is precisely, I think, where we left off last week. The entry at 510: "Milenko Jovanovic to send food and soft drinks to the IKM, the IKM called, Milenko Jovanovic was informed." What did you have to do with that entry in the officer's notebook?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said it, this was a request for certain quantities of foods and drinks to be sent from the command and those were for my men, the men who were at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who was there that morning?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides myself there was the signalsman, security, a driver, and probably Milisav Petkovic, the chief of communications, and I don't know who else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did anybody else arrive during the early part of the morning?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic arrived at forward command post in the early hours of the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: About what time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was soon after 5.00. Sometime between 5.00 and half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you able to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What -- were you alone when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked to be briefed about the events for which he had been sent to Zvornik earlier, and he told me what had happened in Rocevic, Kozluk and Bilici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he had met that evening with Milorad Trbic who was the duty operations officer, Dragan Nikolic wasn't there on that day because his brother had been killed; and Trbic conveyed to him, or rather, confirmed the killings in Orahovaci and Petkovci, also he said that prisoners were accommodated in the schools in Pilici and Rocevici and that they were executed there. And also Trbic told him that Mr. Beara had been in the area and was in charge of that business.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned some machinery from the engineers company and some companies that had been used in order to bury the dead bodies, the bodies of those who had been executed by shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Had he found out any locations where excuses had taken place?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he said that the executions had taken place in the vicinity of Drina, of those from Rocevici, and that those from Pilica had been executed at Branjevo. And that the executions had been carried out by the soldiers from the 10th Sabotage Detachment and some soldiers who had arrived from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Leaving aside what you had told him to go and find out about, did he tell you anything else that had been going on at brigade command during the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He also told me that there had been a number of calls by the corps command of the Main Staff, that even the president of the republic showed interest in the events in Baljkovica, the opening of the corridor, and letting the column of the 28th Division go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did he tell you what the reaction of those people had been to your opening of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we could conclude at that moment was that it was not something of the ordinary, to receive so many calls on one single day from the corps command. And we were aware that our action had not been approved and that there would be more reactions after the initial calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: After you had been briefed by Obrenovic, what did you tell him to do? What did you decide you would do?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since on the previous day the column was going through and this was stopped when the dark fell, it was our plan to continue with the same procedure on the 17th, and in that sense I sent Mr. Obrenovic to the command of the 4th Battalion to make sure that everything was organised there, and to monitor the work of that battalion. And later on I established communication with Semso Muminovic and we continued the process to let the column go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What action did you decide to take about the information Obrenovic had given you about the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that we would resume that conversation later, as soon as our job was over, and our job at hand was to let the column of the 28th Division go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did Dragan Obrenovic go after this conversation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went in the direction of Parlog to the command of the 4th Battalion that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we look now in e-court, please, at P 1206. And the best version of this document is C, but that is under seal in the Serbian, so the appropriate measures will need be to taken. The English is A. I am being corrected, we should use D in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, this is a record of an intercepted radio communication which apparently involves General Krstic, Captain Trbic, and you at about 6.15 on the morning of the 17th of July. Do you recall having a conversation with General Krstic at about 6.15 on the morning of the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's been pointed out to me that the conversations you need to look at actually start at the very bottom of the page. Now, just a couple of things about this conversation. Captain Trbic you've already referred to him in with your evidence this morning. What position was he fulfilling at brigade command on the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the operations GT officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we see in the middle of this conversation that General Krstic appears to ask him: "Do you have communication with your commander?" He says: "Yes. "You have? "Yes. "Good. Put me through to him. "Well, I can't connect you now, you have to go through the switchboard again." "Switchboard." And then General Krstic asks him if he will do that. Can you explain what that aspect of this conversation demonstrates to us?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please be shown the following page in the Serbian version where the conversation continues?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can probably make that easier for you by giving you a hard copy of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this part of the intercept that you are showing me shows that I was at the IKM, and that I could be spoken to via the switchboard, and that's why Krstic had to get in touch with the switchboard and the switchboard in turn established communication with me at the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which report is General Krstic referring to in this conversation that he has initially with Trbic before he is put through to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably meant the interim combat report that I had sent on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so that we can put this conversation into context, is your recollection that you had this conversation before, during, or after your conversation with Dragan Obrenovic on the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was after my conversation with Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you mention your conversation with Dragan Obrenovic to General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on that morning. When we were talking, I expected him to say something about my report that I sent on the 15th or 16th. This did not happen, and I thought it was necessary for me to meet with him in person and to discuss that topic in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What did you do after you'd had this conversation with General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I established communication with Semso Muminovic and we relaunched the process to let the column go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did Semso Muminovic have any particular concerns about the process on the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semso wanted this process to start as soon as possible, and as per our agreement, the corridor should have been opened 24 hours, and during that conversation he suggested that the time should be extended, and that all those who were in the territory of Baljkovica and surrounding area to go through, and we agreed that the dead-line should be extended and that all those who found themselves in the territory on that day would be allowed to let go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go back to the duty officers' notebook for a little while. For you, General Pandurevic, page 774. In e-court that's page 156. And can we have a look at the entry, please, for 8.15 in the morning of the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And there's a linked entry a little further down which begins with the name Miladen Mijatovic, which is substantially to the same effect. Can you explain who gave the order for that to be done and what the purpose of doing it was?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order for Captain Mijatovic to be engaged in calling members of the column of the 28th Division and direct them to the corridor was mine, since the column of the 28th Division was broken up into several parts and Semso had lost communication with most of them, and that's why we had to use the -- we had to use the loud-speakers to call them and to direct them -- direct them in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I just sense, General Pandurevic, that you might be speaking a little bit quickly this morning, so if you could slow down. And while we're there, the entry at the very bottom of that page, 9.30: "Send details of the dead and wounded in an interim combat report to Zlatar. Requested at 9.30." Did you become aware of that request on the morning of the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time that request was communicated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you understand your obligation to be as a result of that request, and what was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd assumed that the Drina Corps asked for information from me as to what had really happened, what were the reasons behind my decisions about the opening of the corridor. However, I decided that on that day I would not send an interim combat report. I decided to hold on and wait and only do it the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like to look at one of the other documents that record events in the brigade, and that's the duty operations officer's diary, P378. In the B/C/S it's page 89, in the English page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if the hard copy is available, I think you'll find, General Pandurevic, you are looking for page 688. Those being the last three digits. I'm sorry, 691. I see. The English translation is 688 of this document, that was my mistake. Now, on the page you are looking at, while we wait for the English to come up, is there an entry for 8.45 in the morning of the 17th of July, which we now have which reads: "A group of commanding officers led by Colonel Trku lja came to the brigade's forward command post in order to review the conditions in new situation and they returned at 1500 hours." Do you have that in front of you, General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall this event?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this team of officers were at the IKM on this day, the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did they first arrive in the area of the brigade so far as you were aware?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I remember, first they arrived in the Parlog area, and their first contact was with Dragan Obrenovic, and then with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How many of them did you meet?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met three of them. Mr. Stankovic and Mr. Sladojevic were people that I saw for the first time at the time, and I knew of Mr. Stankovic. I had -- I never heard of Mr. Sladojevic before. And as for Mr. Trkulja, I'm not sure I had seen him before or not, but in any case I did know that such a person existed at the Main Staff. And I think that perhaps a few moments later Colonel Lazic also appeared, who was in the operations of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the situation on the ground at the time they arrived?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the situation was calm, quiet. The column was in the process of passing through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you understand the purpose of their visit to the brigade's area and the forward command post to be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them expressly told me what the purpose of their visit was, but they told me that they had received certain information from Dragan Obrenovic before about what was happening, but I was able to conclude simply that the purpose of their arrival was to review the justification for my actions, or the absence of thereof.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what form did your meeting with them take?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was just spontaneous. Since I didn't know these two gentlemen, like I said before, I introduced myself to them. I asked them if they needed any other information other than what they had already received from Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you able to conclude whether they had read your combat reports of the previous few days?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask me anything outside of the events that happened in the area of Baljkovica. I really didn't know or had any information if they had received those reports or if anyone had informed them of the contents of those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you say anything to them about prisoners in schools?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure about that event. The logic of it would be for me to say something about it, but at that time I was acting in such a way that I was just giving answers to what I was asked. I didn't really state any of my personal impressions or information or thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why were you behaving like that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they had been sent by the commander of the Main Staff, and that it was better at that point in time for them to receive as little information as possible for me in relation to the reasons why they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were there for a few hours. Since the situation was calm, we were just monitoring the passage of the 28th Division column, all kinds of conversations were going on of an official and personal nature. I was continually in contact with Semso Muminovic, and after the official part, I didn't really participate that much in their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just now have a look at another intercept. It's P112 [sic] A in the English, and C in the B/C/S, which is again under seal. It should say P1221 in the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No great significance to this intercept, General Pandurevic. It's a conversation apparently between the Zlatar duty officer and the Palma duty officer. It's about quarter to 2.00 in the afternoon of the 17th of July, in which the Palma duty officer says that he had just called the commander a little while ago, he is not at the forward command post, he was down in the field, and he couldn't give any information. Help us as to where you were and what you were doing at about quarter to 2.00 in the afternoon of the 17th of July, please?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was immediately above the corridor through which the Muslim forces were passing, and there was no communication between the IKM and me, and that's why the operations officer could not get in touch with me directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, how long had it originally been anticipated that the corridor would be open for?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The original agreement was for 24 hours, so approximately until 1400 hours on the 17th. But this time was extended until 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that the subject of any further negotiation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were in touch, Semso and myself, throughout the whole day, and we saw that there was still people arriving from the woods and we decided to extend the time, and in case certain groups should appear throughout the day, they would be able to pass unhindered through our disposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we get an impression, what did the closure of the corridor practically mean? What actually happened at 1800 hours on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time on the 17th of July, our forces, or rather the soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade, entered those three trenches again that had been emptied earlier, and literally the continuity was -- of the defence line was re-established. Later the minefields were being ordered, the ones that had to be removed when the corridor was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the flow of people like at 1800 hours on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time the people were not passing, and that's when I had a conversation with Semso about the Jankovic capture, the person who was captured, and I asked him to return Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we leave Jankovic to one side for a minute. In your recollection, when had the last groups passed through the corridor prior to its closure?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was sometime between 16 and 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, let's come back to Jankovic. What did you say -- what happened in relation to Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked Semso to release Jankovic, to tell me when he was going to set off, and along which routes so that we could pick him up. He agreed to my request and told me that he had released Jankovic, that he was going down a field, and it's true that we did see a man heading in our direction. However, shortly Semso called again and he told me that he had to return Jankovic because he had received such an order from General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened on the evening of the 17th of July after the corridor had been closed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in particular. All the Zvornik Brigade units remained at their positions, precautionary measures were taken, measures of combat readiness also. I issued assignments to the units for the night. I also issued an assignment to Dragan Obrenovic who had stayed at the IKM overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When and where did you see Obrenovic on the evening of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we met at the IKM, and we discussed that day's activities, and I issued him overnight assignments that were supposed to be completed during his stay at the IKM, and we also talked about the drafting of the interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you say you discussed the day's activities, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the letting through of the column and the visit of the colonels from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you, between you, conclude about the drafting of an interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We concluded that the report should be written on the following day, and that we should just summarise all that had taken place over the previous two or three days, and to also formulate in the appropriate way in the report what we knew about the executions that had taken place in the Zvornik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, well, you've touched on this twice already. Why was it that you wanted to delay the sending of a report which we've already seen had been asked for at 9.30 that morning, the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected that I would perhaps receive some other information or some more information about the events, and also about the format and how to actually draft that report in order to satisfy the request of the corps command, and also to provide rational explanations for our acts, first of all, my action of opening the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you in possession at the forward command post of all the information you needed for the sort of report you wanted to draft?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had enough information in any event that I had received from Dragan Obrenovic, and I had enough information about the actual events in the Baljkovica area because I had taken part in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about brigade losses?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have the exact figures for casualties, even on the 16th. And as far as I can recall, on the 16th I said that there were about ten killed, but I wanted to hear from Mr. Galic who maintained those figures. I wanted to receive the precise information because I believe that the corps command wanted on the basis of the losses to evaluate whether my actions were justified or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did you go on the night of the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the night of the 17th of July I left the IKM. I think that I briefly stopped off at the brigade command, and then after that I went to Celopek to my girlfriend's place which is where I spent most of my free time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we just briefly have a look at page 777 for you, General Pandurevic, in the duty officers' notebook. Page 159 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the page, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At the top of the page in the right-hand corner we see a number 589-991. What or whose number is that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the number of the person that I had gone to visit. And this number often appears in this log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what did you do on the morning of the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning of the 18th of July, I went to Baljkovica again to the command of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the corridor had been closed in the early evening of the 17th, but in practical terms on the morning of the 18th what was the situation for any persons or groups who arrived at Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day on the 18th of July all the groups that had appeared in the Baljkovica area were allowed through our disposition and directed towards Nezuk. I remember well one group of teenagers, or young men of some 18 years of age, a group of perhaps seven to ten of them was at the 4th Battalion command post. Somebody had given them spades, shovels, and told them to dig fortifications for the command post. I immediately told them to stop that. I contacted Semso Muminovic and told them the route along which I was sending him a group of young men and whence they arrived at his end, he was to call me back to let me know if they had all reached that place alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were they left to walk on their own or were they escorted?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the minefields had already been laid in front of our forward sector, I ordered Mr. Jokic, the chief of engineering, that he personally should guide them through the minefield and take them so that they could pass through safely, and this is what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you receive any subsequent communication from Semso Muminovic about the welfare of this group?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as they arrived he called me that all had reached his end safely and that everything was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we take another quick look, please, at the duty operation's officer's notebook. It's the same page you were just looking at. Page 777. Page 159 for the rest of us, it's still on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And at the very bottom of that page we see an entry which reads: "R Battalion reported movements of Muslims. Column towards Crni Vrh, told how to act pursuant to commander's orders." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It mean that is those groups were also being sent to Baljkovica and the 4th Battalion command so that they would be let through our disposition in the direction of Nezuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that we understand this, when the corridor was closed on the 17th of July, what was your belief as to whether they had all got through or not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have precise information about how many of these forces were left, but we knew that in any case there were some groups. We also knew that the Muslim command of the 2nd Corps was trying to infiltrate fresh groups and forces that would link up with the stragglers, and make it possible for them to get through to the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll leave that to one side for a moment. What was the principal task you were engaged in during the day of the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of July I was in Baljkovica for a certain period of time, Obrenovic was also there, and it was his assignment to assist the 4th Battalion command in setting up the command post and the communications. Jokic was also there, the chief of engineers, who was overseeing the mining tasks. And after a brief conversation with each of them, I went to the command and wrote the interim command report. I mean, the interim report on the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the state of the terrain around the 4th Battalion on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of July there were no particular activities of the group -- well, the groups that I mentioned appeared in the area. Some small parts of the Zvornik Brigade were sent to complete the search of the terrain in the Planinci-Cetino Brdo-Pandurica sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were there any sanitation issues?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they were searching the terrain, dead bodies of soldiers who were killed, soldiers of the 28th Division were discovered, and it was necessary to collect the bodies in the broader sector of Motovska Kosa and bury them. I told Obrenovic that they should not be doing that job at that time and that I would ask the chief of the civilian protection from Zvornik that they do that task. However, a certain gentleman by the name of Mirkovic, the head of the Zvornik civilian defence, refused my request, and I later ordered our soldiers to collect the bodies and to bury them in the sector of Motovska Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you now recall what the size of that task was?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall precisely. I was not present when this was done, so I am not able to provide you with any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, before we come on to the irregular combat report of the 18th of July, I just want to ask you to explain to us another document which is our P333. In the Serbian version, General Pandurevic, it's all on the one page. This document bears your signature. Did you write it or dictate it or were you the author of it in any way?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the author of the document in the following sense, I ordered the assistant for morale to draft the information of this kind in order to boost the morale of the fighters by pointing out the successes and results that had been achieved during previous fighting, and I also mentioned the units that had to be cited. This document was later on drafted by Mr. Simic and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to whom was it distributed and how?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was distributed to all the units of the Zvornik Brigade and it was distributed by courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I'm not going to ask you any more about that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But can we come on now, please, to P334.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Firstly, can we just deal with the creation of this document. How did it come to be written, by what method?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dictated this document to Mr. Miomir Tinovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did that take place and at about what time of day?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the command of the Zvornik Brigade around noon on the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This may be a question you've answered already, at least by inference, but why was it necessary on the 18th of July to send an interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been sent already a day earlier, the day before. However, on the 18th of July, I decided to do it because I believed that I had enough information and that I had enough sense to be able to draft the report in an adequate way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we start, please, with paragraph 3 of the report, in which there are three, as it were, separate subparagraphs setting out the losses within the brigade. What was the source of your information for the figures you placed in that paragraph of the report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to losses, as I've already told you, it is the organ for organisation and mobilisation and personnel affairs that monitors losses. At the time it was Mr. -- or rather Major Mihajlo Galic. So when it comes to losses, it was my decision not only to show the losses that we suffered on the 15th and 16th of July or maybe the day before that. I decided to provide a broader overview of our losses to provide the corps with a bit broader picture of the overall situation of the Zvornik Brigade and its engagement in the first half of 1995. Thus, the bullet point in question mentions reversible and irreversible losses, i.e., dead and wounded, in the operations around Srebrenica and Zepa, in the fighting in the zone responsibility of the brigade and outside of it during the Krivaja 95 operation, and so on and so forth. As a result of that the command, the corps command could have realised that the Zvornik Brigade had been under a lot of strain in the course of that year. It seems to me that, or as far as I can remember, I mentioned in this report towards the end that I demanded that my suggestions and proposals should be taken into account with a lot more consideration as of that time on. And I may have been a bit more outspoken than I should have been when I mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: As far as you were aware, the figures for dead, wounded, and missing that you had relating to the combat activities in July, were they accurate and reliable?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first part of bullet point 3 where a reference made is to fighting around Srebrenica, Zepa, and the engagement with the reigning parts of the 28th Division as well as of the 24th and the 25th Brigade -- divisions of the 2nd Corps, is something that I was provided with by Mr. Galic, and so for the missing that turned up later, the rest of the information should be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But when we are looking at the first category of losses which begins with the dead numbered at 27, does that include those who had died in operations Krivaja 1995 and Stupcanica 95, if indeed any did in latter of those two operations?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were dead in Srebrenica as far as I can remember. There were between five and seven. I'm not sure, there were also some ten wounded, and there were also a few wounded at Zepa, but again, I don't know their exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it may be obvious, but if we look at the third category that you've cited there, headed: "During Operation Spreca 95, Krivaja 95, Stupcanica 95, and the Defence of Sarajevo," where the number of dead is put at 69, is that paragraph as it were the total of the two that are above it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had suffered a lot of losses in Spreca 95 operation. This operation lasted for awhile, a lot of soldiers deserted during that period, a lot of them were killed and a lot more wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you set out these losses in this detailed way and to record everything that had happened in the first seven months of the year?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was the way to justify my decision to open the corridor. I wanted to draw the Court's attention from the events that took place on the 16th and make them look back at what had preceded that day, what had happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you have any other purpose in drafting this report in the way that you did on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Different other things are mentioned in the report, and we cannot see them at the moment on the screen. I wanted to make a record of all of that. I wanted this to be recorded, and that's why I drafted the report in the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's come on to paragraph 4 then. Paragraph reads: "The situation in the territory: During the last 10 days or so the municipality of Zvornik has been swamped with Srebrenica Turks. It is inconceivable to me that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools in the municipality, in addition to the 7.000 or so who have fled into the forests. This has created an extremely complex situation and the possibility of the total occupation of Zvornik in conjunction with the forces at the front. These actions have stirred up great discontent among the people, and the general opinion is that Zvornik is to pay the price for the taking of Srebrenica." When you said in your last answer you wanted to make a record of that, what was it you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is the only written trace in any of the official documents of the Zvornik Brigade of the Drina Corps which makes a reference as it were in a euphemistic way what was happening in terms of the execution of the prisoners of war. I believe that the Zvornik and Zvornik municipality did not deserve for something of this sort to happen to them. I wanted to leave a written trail of all that, and the only place where this is recorded is here in this report, and as I was reading other documents issued by the corps, I did not find this anywhere. In my previous report issued on the 15th, I mentioned the prisoners, the corps command never reacted to that, nobody ever told me anything, not with this regard. In the meantime I'd received information from Obrenovic that I have spoken about here, and I believed that for the corps command this was explicit enough and that they should be able to understand what I was talking about. I really could not grasp or understand all that, and there were no words for me to be able to describe what had happened, why, and how.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just on a practical level, remind us what happens when an interim combat report is sent? Does the brigade retain a copy of a combat report that is sent to the corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that would be the one. A typewritten report such as this one. When I left the command of the Zvornik Brigade, i.e., when I handed over my duty, I did not allow for any document to be removed or destroyed in any way. They all remained in the archives of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the copy that is sent, what should happen to that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the corps command on the 17th asked me to write an interim combat report, when they received this report from me, they should have compiled their own interim combat report and copied the contents of this report and incorporate that into that report of theirs, and send their report to the Main Staff. This is what they should have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. But what about the physical copy of the report that you sent to the corps that arrives on their teleprinter, what should happen to that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report that arrives in the corps is printed on the teleprinter in the corps command. The person who does that places his own stamp and records the time and the date when he received the report, and then he hands the report to the authorised person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: On the 18th of July when you dictated this report, did you have any reason to believe, for example, that General Krstic knew anything about the killing operation of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any kind of explicit information that would point to the fact that General Krstic knew something about that. However, I was thinking logically since he had not reacted to my report sent on the 15th, since in the course of the conversation that we conducted in the morning on the 17th, since never happened after my report on the 16th, I fully believed that he was in possession of certain information, but I did not know to what extent he had been informed and what information he was privy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a break now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that will be of 25 minutes duration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, we told you earlier on that after the first break we'll down with two decisions. The first one deals with the urgent joint Defence motion requesting the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to proceed with its cross-examination of co-accused Pandurevic before the joint Defence. This was filed on the 3rd of February. The motion was replied to orally by the Prosecution in the course of the sitting of the 6th February, and we promised to come down with our decisions orally today. In joint motion, the co-accused asked the Trial Chamber to consider the urgent joint Defence motion on an expedited basis, grant the urgent joint Defence motion, and order the Prosecution to proceed with its cross-examination of co-accused Pandurevic before the joint Defence. The Trial Chamber first of all grants the motion insofar as it requests that it be dealt with and decided with urgency. Now, the arguments brought forward by the co-accused are intended to convince the Trial Chamber to depart from the practice regarding the sequence or order of cross-examinations that has been in force following its order regarding the sequence of cross-examination by the parties during the Defence case rendered on 26th of May of last year. The practice before the Trial Chamber, as you know, thus far has been for the Defence teams to conduct their cross-examination of the Defence witnesses, if any, prior to the Prosecution's cross-examination. The main argument of the co-accused is that the testimony of a co-accused in the context of a trial involving multiple accused is different from that of other Defence witnesses. For this reason, the joint Defence submits that the cross-examination of co-accused Pandurevic by the Prosecution must take place prior to the cross-examination of any conducted by the other co-accused. Having examined all the submissions put forward in support of the motion, and particularly the argument that the situation is now different from what it was prior to the 26th May 2008 decision, since the witness is a co-accused, the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that the basic arguments remain the same and that any apparently new submission is, in reality, another way of representing the same arguments heard and determined before -- The Trial Chamber is not convinced that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, would you mind slowing down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber -- all right. So having examined all the submissions put forward in support of the motion, and particularly the argument that the situation is now different from what it was prior to the -- to our 26th May, 2008 decision, since the witness is the co-accused, the Trial Chamber comes to the conclusion that the basic arguments remain the same and that any apparently new submission is in reality another way of representing the same arguments heard and determined before. The Trial Chamber is not convinced that the fact that the current witness is a co-accused should change the effects of its 26th May, 2008, decision which consequently will continue to be operative also in regard to the testimony of the present witness. For these reasons, the motion insofar as it seeks an order to the Prosecution to proceed with the cross-examination of co-accused Pandurevic before the joint Defence is hereby denied. However, as we had pointed out on the previous occasion, should a new issue arise from the Prosecution's cross-examination, Defence teams that have already cross-examined the witness may, upon showing good cause, be permitted to put additional questions to the witness. This will remain the position and the Trial Chamber will consider such request on a case-by-case basis. We now come to our second decision of the day. On the 15th of January of this year, accused Pandurevic filed a request for certification to appeal the Trial Chamber's decision -- Popovic, sorry, accused Popovic filed a request for certification to appeal the Trial Chamber's 14th January oral decision dismissing the Popovic request for guide-lines on the Defence's disclosure obligation of documents obtained during the Defence investigations on the basis that it was of a hypothetical nature. The Prosecution filed a response on the 29th January arguing that Popovic's request for certification does not meet the test for certification under Rule 73(b). The Trial Chamber finds that a decision on granting guide-lines on hypothetical situations is not an issue that would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial. Consequently, the Trial Chamber denies the request for certification to appeal. Mr. Haynes, you can now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We were focusing just before the break on paragraph 4 of your interim combat report of the 18th of July, and it might just be useful if you could reasonably briefly summarise what the state of your knowledge was at the time you dictated that report about the treatment of prisoners in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of July when this report was being written I had the following information available to me: I knew that prisoners of war had been brought to the territory of Zvornik upon the order of the commander of the Main Staff, and that they were actually prisoners of the Main Staff. Further on, I knew that they had been brought in an organised convoy under armed escort, and that this had been organised by the security organs. I also knew that the organisers of that convoy had the authority bestowed upon them by General Mladic. I knew that the prisoners had been accommodated in the facilities which were not military facilities, i.e., facilities which were not within the jurisdiction of the Zvornik Brigade. I knew that there would be no execution on the spot, that there would be the screening followed by an exchange. I knew that the execution or shootings started out of the blue. I didn't have any information to the effect that the Zvornik Brigade had received from the corps any order with regard to the reception of the prisoners or an order with regard to their execution by shooting. I didn't know of any members of the Zvornik Brigade having participated in the execution. And the only thing that I did know to that effect was the fact that Obrenovic placed at Dragan Nikolic's disposal five or six police officers who were to be involved in the reception of the column of the prisoners of war with a view to screening them. I also received information that the machinery BG-H700 from the Zvornik Brigade as well as two other pieces of machinery from public companies had been used at the request of the security organs to bury the dead bodies, the bodies of those who had been executed by shooting. This is more or less the information that I was privy to at the time. In addition to that, I had been informed that members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment had participated in the execution, and also soldiers from Bratunac as well as some other people that were unknown to me. I incorporated that information into my interim combat report on the 18th and I sent it to the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What other courses of action did you consider?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I wrote the report, I also thought about the following: On the 14th the interim combat report arrived from Dragan Obrenovic to the corps command about combat problems. On the 15th I sent a report about problems in combat. No one reacted either on the behalf of the corps or the Main Staff in terms of providing any kind of assistance to the Zvornik Brigade, but when they found out about the opening of the corridor, then three, or rather, four colonels came. I asked myself why didn't they come earlier. That is why I believe that this report written in this form was sufficiently explicit and that General Krstic would know what I was talking about, and I also believed that it was necessary for me to meet with him in person and to speak with him openly about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What authority or ability did you believe on the 18th of July you had to investigate any criminal offences that might have been committed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my duty as the commander, once I learned that a crime had been committed, to inform my superior and then he in turn would inform the prosecutor and the court, and I also had the option to engage the security organs -- or, rather, I knew that the security organs had instructions laid down by the military prosecutor on how to act in legal criminal matters when a crime was committed that was under the jurisdiction of the military court. It was their official duty so that they could launch and conduct an investigation. It would be pointless for me to engage any kind of security organ of the Zvornik Brigade to -- and order them to investigate the crimes in question in which, according to the information that I had, the security organs of the immediately superior and the secondary Superior Command took part. So I did not have the authority to investigate officers from higher commands. All I could do was to inform the corps commander and to expect him to initiate the appropriate mechanisms and to launch an investigation into these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you hope or anticipate General Krstic would do in response to the report you wrote on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I expected that in a way to a certain degree or entirely the contents of my report would be passed on to the Main Staff, or at least he would get back to me and ask me for supplemental information. And then other measures pursuant to the law would be taken when these matters are involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just one minor thing. You've told us what your understanding of the position was in relation to the prisoners in the Zvornik area. Can we just be explicit about the sources of your information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main source of my information was Dragan Obrenovic, and on the 18th in Baljkovica Jokic confirmed to me the engagement of the engineering machinery BGH-700 and one machine from the Birac holding enterprise and one machine from the stone quarry from Josanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Had you by the 18th of July seen any physical evidence to support what Obrenovic had told you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th in the evening when I was returning from the IKM and on my way through Orahovac, I saw that the ground had been disturbed, the earth next to the road from the villages of Krizevci to the village of Orahovac, and I saw that on the 17th in the morning. On the 18th of the morning when I was going back to the IKM, I was not closer than that and I did not visit or tour any of the locations where the executions were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to move on to consider with you what happened to your reports, and could we start please by having a look at P329, very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And all I really want to confirm with you, General Pandurevic, at this stage, is the time at which this report was sent on the 15th of July. So if we can look at the bottom of the document in both the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serbian version on page 2 I think it's 19/2500 hours as far as I can remember from the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful of you and will help us to move on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So I want now, bearing that in mind, to have a look at some Drina Corps reports. And we'll start with P138, the Drina Corps regular combat report for the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I think we can dispense of this document fairly quickly by again just looking at the bottom of it and seeing the time of dispatch of this report to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the time is on the following page, 19/1500 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's read as 19/1500 hours but what you really meant is 19/15; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, can we have a look at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- P150 which is a Drina Corps interim combat report for the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And again let's start by looking at the time that this document was dispatched to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 1945 hours on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So this document was dispatched about 20 minutes after your interim combat report of the 15th of July was sent. If we look at the first page now quickly.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents of this interim combat report of the Drina Corps mostly contains the elements from the regular combat report of the Zvornik Brigade of the 15th of July. There is no information from the interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade from the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think if we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we, just to clarify there's a 2010 under "process," could we explain what that means. This is a document in the Drina Corps, it looks like, signed by someone from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There are two times at the bottom of the report, one is 1945 which appears in the English to be alongside something which says "received," and then there's a time lower down, alongside two words "processed" and "delivered" where the time is 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Pandurevic, can you help us as to why there are two times at the bottom of that Drina Corps document?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try. This report was signed by General Krstic himself, I know his signature. The first time, 1945, is the time when the telegram was received in the encrypted version at the Drina Corps. 2010 hours is when the encryptions person had completed his work and sent the telegram to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were just telling us, which I'm going to demonstrate, that the Drina Corps interim combat report of the 15th of July is pretty much exclusively drawn from the Zvornik Brigade regular combat report of the 15th of July, and if we start looking at the second paragraph, it says: "At about 0440 hours on the 15th of July the enemy started a heavy artillery attack on the 4th, 6th, and 7th Infantry Battalion line of Defence." In the third paragraph it mentions three wounded soldiers called Peric, Stevanovic, and Ristic. And the penultimate paragraphs ends: "... the units which took part in combat operations in the Srebrenica and Zepa sectors returned to brigade zone of responsibility during the day and were involved in operations against enemy groups pulling out of Srebrenica?" With that in mind, can we have a look please at P328. And this is, is it not, the Zvornik Brigade regular combat report of the 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we can see that it begins on the evening of the 14th of July, but if we go to the second paragraph, it says: "On the 15th of July at around 440 hours, the enemy launched a heavy artillery attack on the Defence lines of the 4th, 6th and 7th battalions. The attack ended at 530..." And then in the next paragraph it mentions three wounded soldiers, in this document, called Pekic, Stevanovic and Ristic. And the last substantive paragraph under paragraph 2 reads: "Units which participated in combat activities in the Srebrenica and Zepa areas returned during the day to the brigade area of responsibility and are involved in action against enemy groups retreating from Srebrenica." And it's by reference to that, is it, that you conclude that the interim combat report of the 15th of July sent by the Drina Corps is pretty much a verbatim copy of the regular combat report sent by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you glean from the Drina Corps report, interim combat report of the 15th of July, any information that you sent to them in your interim combat report of the 15th of July at 25 past 7.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the information pretty much overlaps, because the information from the interim report of the Zvornik Brigade of the 15th of July and the regular combat report of the 15th of July does overlap to a certain extent. There are no other elements from the interim combat report of the 15th of July there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's move on a day and have a look at P139, please. The Drina Corps regular combat report of the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I should perhaps just ask you this: That in relation to what we saw by comparing those two documents, the Zvornik Brigade regular combat report of the 15th July, and the Drina Corps interim combat report of the 15th of July, is that what you would expect to happen with information that you sent to your corps command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the regular report of the 15th of July was somewhat late, so probably the regular combat report of the Drina Corps to the Main Staff was dispatched before, and that is why they - when I say "they" I mean the Drina Corps - wrote their own interim combat report on the basis of the regular combat report of the Zvornik Brigade of the -- for the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, here we come to the Drina Corps regular combat report of the 16th of July said to be urgent. Can we go through the same exercise, please. Let's just look at the dates and times which it was received and processed at the bottom of the document which is page 3 in the English?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that the report of the 16th of July arrived at 1637 hours and it was encrypted meaning that it had been written a minute or 10 minutes before that, before it arrived at the encryption station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes. Mr. Haynes, I'm just not clear, the record says - and I heard - 1637, but I'm seeing 1937.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What is the time that the document was received according to you, General Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can see it's 1937 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to the top of that document, we can see that it begins by reporting that: "The enemy has grouped large forces before the front defence lines of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade on the Tuzla-Zvornik axis and launched a very strong artillery infantry attack in the early morning hours against the defence sector of our units from the Baljkovica-Rijeka-Pandurica axis. The enemy is coordinating action with forces pulling out from the former enclave of Srebrenica in an attempt to break through our defence line and thereby create conditions to withdraw a large number of armed soldiers and civilians from the Kamenica sector via Crni Vrh, Cetino Brdo, and Baljkovica..." This is a report sent on the evening of the 16th of July. How accurately does that reflect the military situation in the Drina Corps area of responsibility at that time.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it reflects to a large degree what is written in the interim report of the Zvornik Brigade of the 15th of July. Could we please scroll up so that I could see paragraph 2 about what the Zvornik Brigade is doing? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there was a mistake, probably translation. In fact, I'm sure it was translation seeing my B/C/S person nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In terms of the numbers, the date I believe is what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it says the 15th report, I think he meant -- I think he actually said the 16th report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask him because I don't think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does this Drina Corps report of the 16th of July reflect information which you had given on the 15th or the 16th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade of the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now that the document is scrolled down, we can see just above paragraph 2, Combat Readiness, that the report reads: "According to reports submitted by subordinate units, there are around 3.000 armed soldiers and civilians in the Pandurica, Planinci, Crni Vrh, and Glodjansko Brdo sector." And then under Combat Readiness: "All corps units are in a state of full combat readiness. The 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade with attached units blocked the Crni Vrh, Planinci, and partly the Kamenica sector where large enemy units and numerous civilians moving from Srebrenica over Glodjansko Brdo in the direction of Krizevici are located." We'll leave that there for a minute because I want to finish with this document before, as it were, drawing the comparison. But can we read down through the whole of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if there's an unmarked B/C/S copy for the general, it would be simpler than scrolling down through e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you've read through this, would you tell us whether this Drina Corps report of the 16th of July makes any mention of prisoners in schools?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This regular combat report of the 16th of the Drina Corps command does not mention the prisoners of war in schools, but it only talks about the situation in the front in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if we can now quickly go to the well-known document P329.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And rather than direct your attention to the whole document, just the first paragraph, and see if we can find some familiar words. "There are about 3.000 armed and unarmed enemy soldiers, brigade forces are sealing off and searching the aforementioned region. A few hundred enemy soldiers have so far been liquidated in the territory of the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade area of responsibility in the wider area of Pandurica, Planinci, Crni Vrh, Kamenica, and Glodjansko Brdo." And then down in the third paragraph: "With all available forces we have sealed off the wider area of Crni Vrh, Planinci, and partially the area of Kamenica." So in which report do we find that information reported by the Drina Corps to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll find this information in the regular combat report issued by the Drina Corps on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's move on please. Can we look at P140, the Drina Corps regular combat report of the 17th of July. And again, if we can go straight to the bottom of the report to have a look at the received and processed times.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Received at 1940, processed at 1952 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you just remind us what time of day it was that you sent the interim combat report on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of July, I sent the interim combat report from the Zvornik Brigade at a 2010. As far as I can remember, we had some problems with the encryption device, but that was one day earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we can go to the top of this document and have the opportunity probably all to read it through, and I will simply address two questions to you. Do we find anywhere in this Drina Corps report of the 17th of July any references to prisoners in schools in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see there is none.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do we find anywhere in this Drina Corps report of the 17th of July any reference to the opening of the corridor to allow the forces of the 28th Division through to Nezuk?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's move on a day, shall we, and let's have a look, please, at P141; the Drina Corps regular combat report of the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for this document to come up, you've not long ago given the evidence, but just remind us what time of day it was that you sent your interim combat report on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that report was sent around 1300 hours. Maybe a minute later, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go through the regular practice then, please, of identifying at the bottom of this document, and somebody is thinking ahead of me, I can see, the date and time that this document was received and processed in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document issued by the Drina Corps, the regular combat report for the 18th of July was received at 1900 hours and processed at 1946 hours, and I believe that a few minutes later it arrived at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So that would be something like six hours after you sent your interim combat report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, I'm sure we can all take the time and trouble to read through it, I'm not going to read it all out to you, but in that report is there any mention of prisoners in schools in the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is there any mention of the opening of the corridor by you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is there any mention of losses that the Zvornik Brigade had suffered?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Could you please scroll up a little. No, losses in the Zvornik Brigade are not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's just complete the picture, shall we, and have a look at P151, the Drina Corps interim combat report of the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, just very briefly let's have a look at the bottom of that document at the time it was received and processed.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Received at 1535 on 18 of July, and processed at either 1550 or 1556, I am not sure, which is before the regular combat report for the 18th of July was sent by the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we go back to the top, what I'm going to do, General Pandurevic, is not read from this document, but I'm going to read from your document, P334, your interim combat report of the 18th of July, which reads as follows: "On the 17th of July, the enemy carried out offensive low intensity combat activities in the 7th Battalion area of defence with occasional artillery fire on the right wing of the brigade area of responsibility." How does that correspond to the first paragraph of the Drina Corps report of the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have just read out from the interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade for the 18th of July has been incorporated in the interim combat report by the Drina Corps on the same day, on the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The second paragraph of your report reads: "The Zvornik Brigade forces reinforced by a company from the Krajina 16th Brigade, a company from Bratunac, two platoons of the Bijeljina military police, and one platoon from the Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade successfully repulsed all enemy attacks from the front." How does that correspond to paragraph 2 or the beginning thereof of the Drina Corps report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again this was taken from the interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade and incorporated into the interim combat report of the Drina Corps for the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 of your report reads: "In combat activities with Muslim forces in Srebrenica, Zepa, with parts that remain behind as well as with the forces of the 24th and 25th Infantry Division of the 2nd Corps of the so-called BH Army, the Zvornik Infantry Brigade sustained losses as follows: Dead 27; seriously wounded, 24; slightly wounded, 72." How does that correspond with the report that the Drina Corps sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, like in the previous two cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Paragraph 4 of your report reads: "During the last ten days or so the municipality of Zvornik has been swamped with Srebrenica Turks. It is inconceivable to me that someone brought in 3.000 Turks of military age and placed them in schools of the municipalities in addition to the 7.000 or so who have fled into the forests." How does that corresponds with the report that the Drina Corps sent to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 4 from the interim combat report of the Zvornik Brigade was not incorporated into the interim combat report of the Drina Corps for the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, General Pandurevic, you've spent a lifetime in the army, can you imagine why your corps commander would not have included that paragraph from your report in his report to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a Superior Command, when they draft their report - and I'm talking here about the Drina Corps - that sent its reports to the Main Staff, cannot incorporate everything from the reports of the subordinated units. They compile their own reports and point out the most important things to do with combat operations. However, in any case, the things that are mentioned under item 4 of the Zvornik Brigade for the 18th of July is something that should have found a place in the report of the Drina Corps that was sent to the Main Staff. As we have seen here, that paragraph is simply missing from that report, and thought by the experience of my work in the army, I can conclude that General Krstic had been aware of this even before my report arrived. Also, I can conclude that General Krstic that -- knew that his superior, the one who he was supposed to report to, was also aware of the situation, and in my view, that would be the only reason for him not to include my information into his information. Or maybe he had reasons unknown to me, known only to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were you under any orders not to mention the existence of prisoners in any reports you wrote?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never received any such order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Why did you mention them in the 18th of July report?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I believed that this was important and that this is something that should be reported on and also that should be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to leave that topic and discuss something rather more specific about your report of the 18th of July, and I'd like again, please, to look at P334, the interim combat report of the 18th of July, and just look at the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like to focus, please, General Pandurevic, on the last few lines of the first paragraph of that report which read: "The enemy sustained serious losses and dozens have been captured. In fighting with our forces they showed the utmost impudence, unexpected moves, and an animal instinct for survival. Forces from the front are still determined to coordinate action in enabling the withdrawal of the remaining groups at any cost. Increased combat activity may be expected in the afternoon." When you talk in that couple of sentences about unexpected moves and an animal instinct for survival, did you have any particular incidents in mind?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I received this type of information from Mijo Dragutinovic who spent some time covering the grounds before we drafted this report, and there were -- there was a case when enemy soldiers were taken prisoners. One soldier activated a hand-grenade and one of our soldiers was either killed or seriously injured. In any case, I know that on that occasion one of our soldiers lost an eye.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In the wake of that, did you give any particular orders to your forces?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An order was in place that during the scouring of the terrain, all those who surrendered should be treated fairly in compliance with all the conventions and that they should be transported to the barracks in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to have a look very briefly please at a military document, at text P409, B/C/S page 57 and English page 63. Article 213.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which reads: "Capture. It is prohibited to wound or kill a member of the enemy armed forces from the moment he stops offering resistance and visibly shows that he is willing to surrender, or when due to wounding or sickness, he is not capable of fighting.
